2.7 The Open Economy

The balance of payments

Section titled “The balance of payments”

All of a country’s transactions with the rest of the world are recorded in the balance of payments, which has two main parts:

  • The current account: exports minus imports of goods and services (the net exports NXNXNX of 2.1 Macroeconomic Data), plus net investment income from abroad (interest, dividends) and net transfers.
  • The financial account: net purchases and sales of assets (stocks, bonds, factories, deposits) between residents and foreigners.

The two are two sides of the same thing. When the United States imports more than it exports, the difference has to be paid with something: by selling dollar assets (Treasury bonds, stocks, real estate) to foreigners. So a current account deficit always comes with an equal net capital inflow from abroad (apart from statistical errors).

The current account can also be seen through saving and investment. From Y=C+I+G+NXY = C + I + G + NXY=C+I+G+NX, national saving is S=Y−C−GS = Y - C - GS=Y−C−G (ignoring net investment income and transfers), so

S−I=NXS - I = NXS−I=NX

When a country saves less than it invests, the difference must be borrowed from abroad, and the current account is in deficit. A current account deficit is not necessarily bad: for a country with many investment opportunities, borrowing from abroad to invest makes sense; but if the deficit comes from consumption and government deficits, it must be repaid with future output.

In 2025 the US current account deficit was about 1.12 trillion dollars, 3.6% of GDP; at the end of 2025 the net foreign liabilities of the United States (its net international investment position) were about 27.54 trillion dollars (BEA, released March 25, 2026).

A country with a current account deficit must be in poor economic shape.

Exchange rates

Section titled “Exchange rates”

The nominal exchange rate is the rate at which two currencies exchange. In this lesson EEE is the number of dollars per unit of foreign currency; for example, a euro exchange rate of E=1.10E = 1.10E=1.10 means 1 euro buys 1.10 dollars. A rise in EEE means the foreign currency appreciates and the dollar depreciates.

The nominal rate alone is not enough: if the euro rises 5% but US prices rise 5% at the same time while European prices stay the same, US goods have not become cheaper relative to European goods. To compare the relative prices of two countries’ goods, use the real exchange rate:

ε=E P∗P\varepsilon = \frac{E\,P^*}{P}ε=PEP∗​

where PPP is the US price level and P∗P^*P∗ the foreign price level (in foreign currency). When ε\varepsilonε rises, foreign goods become relatively dearer, US goods become more competitive, exports rise and imports fall.

Exchange rates are set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market: when demand for dollar assets rises (for example, because US interest rates rise, 2.5 Monetary Policy), the dollar appreciates.

Purchasing power parity

Section titled “Purchasing power parity”

If the same good has different prices in two countries (after conversion to the same currency), one can buy where it is cheap and sell where it is dear. This arbitrage pushes prices toward equality and is called the law of one price. Applied to the whole price level, it gives purchasing power parity (PPP): the exchange rate makes the purchasing power of the two currencies equal, E=PP∗E = \frac{P}{P^*}E=P∗P​, so the real exchange rate is ε=1\varepsilon = 1ε=1.

More useful is its form in rates of change (relative PPP):

ΔEE≈π−π∗\frac{\Delta E}{E} \approx \pi - \pi^*EΔE​≈π−π∗

The currency of the country with higher inflation depreciates, roughly offsetting the difference in inflation.

PPP is very inaccurate in the short run: many goods and services (rent, haircuts) cannot be traded across borders, transport is costly, and exchange rates are strongly affected by capital flows and expectations, so the real exchange rate can stay away from 1 for years. But in the long run, especially for countries with very different inflation rates, it is a useful reference for exchange rate trends.

Check C2
Suppose US inflation is 3% a year from now on and euro-area inflation 2%. By relative purchasing power parity, in the long run:
US prices rise faster, so a dollar buys less and less. To keep purchasing power equal across the two, should the dollar rise or fall?
If the nominal rate stays put while US prices rise faster, do US goods become dearer or cheaper?
Euro-area prices are rising too. Which part of inflation should the exchange rate offset?

Interest parity

Section titled “Interest parity”

A US investor with 1 dollar can buy a 1-year US Treasury bill at the interest rate iii; or convert to euros, buy a 1-year euro government bond at the rate i∗i^*i∗, and convert back to dollars after a year.

If today the investor fixes the rate for converting back in a year with a forward contract at the rate FFF, there is no currency risk. The two risk-free investments must give the same return, or there would be risk-free arbitrage. So

FE=1+i1+i∗\frac{F}{E} = \frac{1 + i}{1 + i^*}EF​=1+i∗1+i​

This is called covered interest parity. It usually holds approximately between major currencies. It means that a higher foreign interest rate does not mean earning more after hedging; the higher rate is offset by the forward discount.

Without a forward contract, the return depends on the spot rate a year later and is risky. If investors did not care about this risk, the two investments would also have the same expected return:

ΔEeE≈i−i∗\frac{\Delta E^e}{E} \approx i - i^*EΔEe​≈i−i∗

where ΔEe\Delta E^eΔEe is the expected change in the exchange rate. That is, the currency with the higher interest rate is expected to depreciate by about the interest differential. This is called uncovered interest parity. Empirical studies find that it often fails in the short run: high-rate currencies on average depreciate less than this, or even appreciate. The “carry trade”, borrowing in a low-rate currency and investing in a high-rate currency, therefore earns money on average, but in a crisis the high-rate currency can suddenly fall sharply and cause large losses (Exercises Question 3).

Check C3
The 1-year dollar rate is 4% and the euro rate 2%. A US investor buys a 1-year euro government bond and fully hedges the currency risk with a forward contract. In dollars, his return is about:
When hedging, is the forward rate the same as the spot rate? By covered interest parity, is the forward rate above or below spot?
If hedging gave 6%, borrowing dollars, buying euro bonds and hedging would earn 2% without risk. Would such a chance last?
After hedging with a forward, at what rate are euros changed back in a year? Is that rate fixed today or known only in a year?

Currency risk

Section titled “Currency risk”

When investing in foreign assets, the return in home currency has two parts:

1+R=(1+R∗) (1+x)1 + R = (1 + R^*)\,(1 + x)1+R=(1+R∗)(1+x)

where R∗R^*R∗ is the return in foreign currency and xxx is the change in the foreign currency against the home currency. Even if the foreign stocks themselves do well, a fall in the foreign currency can eat up much of the return.

Should currency risk be hedged?

  • Currency hedging (with forward contracts and the like) removes most currency fluctuations; by covered interest parity, the cost or gain of hedging is about the interest differential between the two countries.
  • Not hedging adds currency fluctuations to the portfolio’s risk, but the correlation coefficient between the currency and the foreign asset’s return matters: if the foreign currency tends to rise when the foreign stock market falls, not hedging can even lower risk.

For stocks, currency effects partly cancel out in the long run, and many investors hedge part of their exposure; for bonds, currency swings are often much larger than the bonds’ own swings, so foreign bonds are usually hedged (Exercises Question 5).

Check C4
A US investor holds Japanese stocks. Over a year, the return in yen is 10% and the yen falls 8% against the dollar. His return in dollars is exactly 2%.
Does the yen's 8% fall apply only to the principal, or also to the 10% gain? Work out (1+R∗)(1+x)−1(1 + R^*)(1 + x) - 1(1+R∗)(1+x)−1.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Current account ≈ net exports plus net investment income; a current account deficit comes with an equal net capital inflow. S−I=NXS - I = NXS−I=NX. The US current account deficit in 2025 was about 1.12 trillion dollars, 3.6% of GDP.
  • The nominal exchange rate EEE is the home-currency price of one unit of foreign currency; the real exchange rate ε=EP∗P\varepsilon = \frac{EP^*}{P}ε=PEP∗​ compares the relative prices of two countries’ goods.
  • Relative PPP: ΔEE≈π−π∗\frac{\Delta E}{E} \approx \pi - \pi^*EΔE​≈π−π∗; inaccurate in the short run, a useful reference in the long run.
  • Covered interest parity: FE=1+i1+i∗\frac{F}{E} = \frac{1 + i}{1 + i^*}EF​=1+i∗1+i​, so a hedged foreign investment earns the home interest rate. Uncovered interest parity often fails in the short run; carry trades earn money on average but can crash.
  • The home-currency return on a foreign asset is (1+R∗)(1+x)−1(1 + R^*)(1 + x) - 1(1+R∗)(1+x)−1; hedging costs about the interest differential, and whether to hedge depends on currency volatility and its correlation with the asset’s return.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A country's GDP is 100, national saving 20 and investment 23 (ignore net investment income and transfers), so the current account deficit is 3.
(a) A new technology raises business investment to 25, with saving unchanged. What is the current account balance now? What do foreigners get in exchange for the extra goods?
(b) The government announces tariffs on imports. If saving and investment do not change, does the current account balance change in the long run? Why?
Question 2 ★
Over a year, the euro rises 10% against the dollar (EEE up 10%), US prices rise 6% and euro area prices 1%.
(a) By what percentage does the real exchange rate ε=EP∗P\varepsilon = \frac{EP^*}{P}ε=PEP∗​ change?
(b) Have US goods become more competitive relative to European goods? Why does the change in the nominal rate overstate this?
Question 3 ★
An investor borrows yen (at 0.5% a year), converts them to dollars and buys 1-year US Treasuries (at 4% a year), unhedged, converting back to yen after a year to repay the loan.
(a) By how much at most can the dollar fall against the yen for the trade not to lose money?
(b) If uncovered interest parity holds, what is the expected return of this trade? Why does it make money on average in practice, yet is compared to "picking up coins in front of a steamroller"?
Question 4
A country has inflation of 20% a year, the US 3%. The country's 1-year government bond rate is 24%.
(a) By relative PPP (in exact form), by about how much does the country's currency fall against the dollar each year?
(b) An investment product advertises "a 24% yearly return, far above US Treasuries". Using the Fisher equation and covered interest parity, explain why this is not a "free lunch".
